QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r1.claim: The Prophet asks how one could take another Muslim's property without right if God prevents the fruit from growing.
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r1.anchor: أرأيت إن منع الله الثمرة فبم يأخذ أحدكم مال أخيه بغير حق

QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r2.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r2.claim: The majority invalidate a sale of fruit before ripening when the buyer must leave it on the tree; Abu Hanifa and his companions regard the prohibition as disapproval instead.
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r2.anchor: هذا قول الجمهور، وصححه أبو حنيفة وأصحابه وحملوا النهي على الكراهة.

QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r3.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r3.claim: The majority permit pre-ripening sale if the fruit is to be cut immediately, reasoning by clear analogy that it is known and deliverable at contracting; al-Thawri and Ibn Abi Layla prohibit it under the report's general wording.
QURTUBI-FULL:6:99#5/r3.anchor: وذهب الجمهور إلى جواز بيعها قبل بدو الصلاح بشرط القطع. ومنعه الثوري وابن أبي ليلى

QASHANI:6:99/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r1.claim: Rain from the spirit’s heaven is the water of knowledge, which brings forth every class of moral quality and virtue.
QASHANI:6:99/r1.anchor: ماء العلم { فأخرجنا به نبات } كل صنف من الأخلاق والفضائل

QASHANI:6:99/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r2.claim: The green growth is the soul’s fresh, verdant form, beautified and gladdened by knowledge and character.
QASHANI:6:99/r2.anchor: من النبات هيئة خضرة النفس وزينة حسنة جميلة وبهجة بالعلم والخلق

QASHANI:6:99/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r3.claim: The grains are ordered, noble, accepted deeds and sincere intentions that strengthen the heart.
QASHANI:6:99/r3.anchor: أعمالا مترتبة شريفة مرضية، ونيات صادقة يتقوى بها القلب

QASHANI:6:99/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r4.claim: The date palm is the intellect; as its attachments emerge, it yields accessible knowledge and truths made nearly self-evident by spirit-light.
QASHANI:6:99/r4.anchor: ومن نخل العقل من ظهور تعلقها معارف وحقائق قريبة التناول لظهورها بنور الروح كأنها بديهية

QASHANI:6:99/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r5.claim: Grape gardens signify spiritual states and tastes, especially kinds of heart-love whose juice and pure wine intoxicate.
QASHANI:6:99/r5.anchor: الأحوال والأذواق وخصوصا أنواع المحبة القلبية المسكر عصيرها وسلافها

QASHANI:6:99/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r6.claim: Olives represent reflection, while pomegranates represent true conjectures, lofty aspirations, and precious resolve.
QASHANI:6:99/r6.anchor: وزيتون التفكر، ورمان التوهمات الصادقة التي هي الهمم الشريفة

QASHANI:6:99/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r7.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r7.claim: Some fruits resemble one another, like intellectual reflection, knowledge, deeds, intentions, or love of essence and attributes; others differ, including kinds of love and their ranks, strength, and visibility.
QASHANI:6:99/r7.anchor: كالتعقلات والتفكرات والمعارف والحقائق والأعمال والنيات

QASHANI:6:99/r8.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r8.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r8.claim: During the path and the beginning of a spiritual state, one should watch its fruit through vigilant self-observation and turn attention from pleasures toward these fruits.
QASHANI:6:99/r8.anchor: وليكن نظركم من اللذات إلى هذه الثمرات

QASHANI:6:99/r9.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r9.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r9.claim: Ripening signifies perfection at arrival through spiritual presence.

QASHANI:6:99/r10.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:6:99/r10.speaker: author
QASHANI:6:99/r10.claim: These are signs for those with knowledge-based faith who affirm the enumerated signs and spiritual states.
QASHANI:6:99/r10.anchor: ويوقنون هذه الآيات والأحوال التي عددناها

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r1.claim: The account of rain and vegetation is a fifth proof of God’s power, knowledge, wisdom, mercy, and beneficence toward creation.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r1.anchor: هذا النوع الخامس من الدلائل الدالة على كمال قدرة الله تعالى وعلمه وحكمته

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r2.claim: These signs are also complete blessings; combining proof with beneficence strongly affects the heart, so callers to truth should use this approach.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r2.anchor: الدلائل كما أنها دلائل فهي أيضا نعم بالغة

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r3.claim: Razi introduces the apparent implication that water descends from the sky and notes that people disagree about it.

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r4.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r4.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi says God sends water from the sky to clouds, then from clouds to earth, retaining the apparent wording absent proof against it.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r4.anchor: قال أبو علي الجبائي في ( تفسيره ) : إنه تعالى ينزل الماء من السماء إلى السحاب

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r5.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r5.claim: Against the vapor account of rain, al-Jubbaʾi argues that hail in summer and liquid rain in the coldest weather contradict its explanation.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r5.anchor: احتج الجبائي على فساده من وجوه : الأول : أن البرد قد يوجد في وقت الحر

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r6.speaker: القوم
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r6.claim: Proponents reply that summer heat drives cold into the vapor-rich cloud and concentrates it into hail, whereas winter cold outside prevents inner freezing so rain falls as water.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r6.anchor: القوم يجيبون عنه فيقولون : لا شك أن البخار أجزاء مائية

RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r7.claim: Razi counters that if the upper air is very cold, winter’s cold upper and lower air should prevent rain altogether, contrary to observation.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86/r7.anchor: يمكن أن يجاب عنه بأن الطبقة العالية من الهواء باردة جدا عندكم

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r1.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r1.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi’s second argument says dispersed rising vapors cannot form droplets without a smooth continuous ceiling, such as glazed bathhouse roofs.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r1.anchor: الحجة الثانية : مما ذكره الجبائي أنه قال : إن البخارات إذا ارتفعت

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r2.speaker: القوم
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r2.claim: The vapor proponents answer that cold air makes dispersed vapor heavy and descend; on a spherical world the particles converge and join into raindrops.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r2.anchor: القوم يجيبون عنه : بأن هذه البخارات إذا تصاعدت وتفرقت

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r3.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r3.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi’s third argument is that continuously rising sea vapors should cause continuous rainfall, which is not observed.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r3.anchor: الحجة الثالثة : ما ذكره الجبائي قال : لو كان تولد المطر

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r4.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r4.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi attributes the vapor theory to belief in eternal bodies, where events are only atoms acquiring new qualities, and each thing must arise from preexisting matter.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r4.anchor: والقوم إنما احتاجوا إلى هذا القول

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r5.claim: Muslims hold that bodies are originated and the willing, powerful Creator makes them as He wills, removing the need for such strained natural explanations.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r5.anchor: وأما المسلمون . فلما اعتقدوا أن الأجسام محدثة

RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r6.claim: Other verses likewise say water or hail descends from the sky; Razi concludes God creates rain in the sky, then it descends through cloud to earth.
RAZI-FULL:v13p86#2/r6.anchor: جميع الآيات ناطقة بنزول المطر من السماء

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r1.claim: A second view takes the phrase to mean that rain is sent from the direction of the sky.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r1.anchor: والقول الثاني : المراد إنزال المطر من جانب السماء

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r2.claim: A third view says water is sent from clouds, which God calls sky because Arabs use sky for anything above, as with a house ceiling.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r2.anchor: والقول الثالث : أنزل من السحاب ماء

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r3.claim: Al-Wahidi transmits from Ibn Abbas that the water here is rain and every raindrop is accompanied by an angel.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r3.anchor: نقل الواحدي في ( البسيط ) عن ابن عباس : يريد بالماء ههنا المطر

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r4.speaker: الفلاسفة
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r4.claim: Philosophers interpret the accompanying angel as the nature inherent in the body that causes its descent; Razi says a heavenly angel accompanying it is difficult to affirm.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r4.anchor: الفلاسفة يحملون ذلك الملك على الطبيعة الحالة في تلك الجسمية الموجبة لذلك النزول

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r5.claim: The surface wording that God brings plants out by water implies natural causation, which theologians reject; Razi refers back to his discussion at 2:22.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r5.anchor: يدل على أنه تعالى إنما أخرج النبات بواسطة الماء

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r6.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r6.claim: Al-Farraʾ restricts the phrase’s apparent universal meaning to plants of things that actually have plants; things without vegetation are excluded.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r6.anchor: قال الفراء : قوله : { فأخرجنا به نبات كل شيء } ظاهره يقتضي أن يكون لكل شيء نبات

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r7.claim: Changing from the second-person address in anzala to the first-person plural in fa-akhrajna is iltifat; Razi says its rhetorical basis was treated at 10:22.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r7.anchor: يسمى التفاتا . ويعد ذلك من الفصاحة

RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r8.claim: The plural form refers to God, who is one, by the convention that a great ruler speaks of himself in the plural.
RAZI-FULL:v13p87/r8.anchor: صيغة الجمع . والله واحد فرد لا شريك له

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r1.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r1.claim: Al-Zajjaj says khadir means akhdar, green, with a shortened adjective form comparable to aʿwar and ʿawar.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r1.anchor: قال الزجاج : معنى خضر ، كمعنى أخضر

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r2.speaker: الليث
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r2.claim: Al-Layth says khidr in the Qurʾan means grain crop, though in ordinary speech it can mean any green plant.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r2.anchor: قال الليث : الخضر في كتاب الله هو الزرع

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r3.claim: Since 6:95 divides plants into what grows from grain and from date stones, Razi takes khadir here as the crop from grain, following al-Layth’s sense.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r3.anchor: اعتبر هذه القسمة أيضا في هذه الآية فابتدأ بذكر الزرع

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the crops as wheat, barley, sult, maize, and rice, and khadir as the first green stalk with an ear at its top.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r4.anchor: قال ابن عباس : يريد القمح والشعير والسلت والذرة والأرز

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r5.claim: The stacked grains grow one above another in a single ear.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r5.anchor: يعني يخرج من ذلك الخضر حبا متراكبا بعضه على بعض في سنبلة واحدة

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r6.claim: The tiny sharp bodies above the ear are created to prevent birds from picking the stacked grains.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r6.anchor: ويحصل فوق السنبلة أجسام دقيقة حادة كأنها الأبر

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r7.claim: After plants from grain, the verse turns to the second category, plants from date stones: palms.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r7.anchor: ولما ذكر ما ينبت من الحب أتبعه بذكر ما ينبت من النوى

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r8.claim: Razi reports an argument that mentioning grain crops before palms indicates crops are superior; al-Jahiz wrote a lengthy work on this question.

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda says a palm produces its talʿ; the spathes are like cases before opening, and talʿ is the first visible part of a palm cluster, singular talʿa.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r9.anchor: روى الواحدي عن أبي عبيدة أنه قال : أطلعت النخل إذا أخرجت طلعها

RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r10.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r10.claim: Al-Zajjaj says qinwan is the plural of qinw, like sunwan from sunw; its form resembles the dual, while the n-un inflection marks the plural.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88/r10.anchor: قال الزجاج : القنوان جمع قنو . مثل صنوان وصنو

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the near clusters as hanging palm bunches close enough to pick.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس : يريد العراجين التي قد تدلت من الطلع دانية ممن يجتنيها

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r2.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas takes them as short palms whose clusters cling close to the ground.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r2.anchor: وروى عنه أيضا أنه قال : قصار النخل اللاصقة عذوقها بالأرض

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r3.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that distant bunches are omitted because mentioning one of two opposites implies the other, as in garments protecting from heat without naming cold.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r3.anchor: قال الزجاج : ولم يقل ومنها قنوان بعيدة لأن ذكر أحد القسمين يدل على الثاني

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r4.claim: Another explanation singles out near bunches because their closeness makes the blessing greater and more abundant.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r4.anchor: وقيل أيضا : ذكر الدانية في القريبة

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r5.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r5.claim: Al-Kashshaf parses qinwan as a nominative subject with min al-nakhl as predicate and min talʿiha as apposition; alternatively its predicate is omitted and inferred from akhrajna.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r5.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) { قنوان } رفع بالابتداء

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r6.claim: For readers who have yukhraju minhu habb, qinwan is coordinated with habb; qinwan is also read with qaf either damma or fatha as a collective noun.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r6.anchor: ومن قرأ يخرج منه { حب } كان { طلعها قنوان } عنده

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r7.speaker: عاصم
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r7.claim: Asim, also reported as Ali’s reading, has nominative jannat; the others read it in the accusative, with differing syntactic explanations.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r7.anchor: قرأ عاصم : { جنات } بضم التاء ، وهي قراءة علي رضي الله عنه

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r8.claim: The nominative may mean gardens are alongside the palms or coordinate with qinwan as what is produced; the accusative coordinates with نبات كل شيء, while al-Kashshaf prefers specification for the especially fine olives and pomegranates.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r8.anchor: أما القراءة الأولى فلها وجهان : الأول : أن يراد

RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r9.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r9.claim: Al-Farraʾ says olive and pomegranate refer to their trees, as ask the village means ask its inhabitants.
RAZI-FULL:v13p88#2/r9.anchor: قال الفراء : قوله : { والزيتون والرمان } يريد شجر الزيتون

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r1.claim: The order puts crops before trees because grain is food, while tree produce is fruit and food precedes fruit.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r1.anchor: قدم الزرع على الشجر لأن الزرع غذاء ، وثمار الأشجار فواكه

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r2.claim: The date palm precedes other fruit trees because dates serve Arabs as food and philosophers note its unusual resemblance to animals in many properties.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r2.anchor: قدم النخل على سائر الفواكه لأن التمر يجري مجرى الغذاء بالنسبة إلى العرب

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r3.claim: A prophetic saying calls the palm the paternal aunt of plants and says it was created from what remained of Adam's clay; Razi gives no grading.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r3.anchor: قال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( أكرموا عمتكم النخلة

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r4.claim: Razi calls grape king of fruits: its shoots, sour unripe grapes and ripe fruit each have uses; hanging grapes store well and yield raisins, syrup, wine and vinegar; wine is forbidden despite acknowledged benefit (2:219), and seed preparations aid weak moist stomachs.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r4.anchor: فثبت أن العنب كأنه سلطان الفواكه

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r5.claim: Olives are useful eaten whole and also yield abundant oil for food and many other uses.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r5.anchor: يمكن تناوله كما هو ، وينفصل أيضا عنه دهن كثير عظيم النفع

RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r6.claim: A pomegranate is a compound body with four parts: rind, pith, seeds and juice.
RAZI-FULL:v13p89/r6.anchor: جسم مركب من أربعة أقسام : قشره وشحمه وعجمه وماؤه

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r1.claim: The rind, pith and seeds are dense, cold, dry, earthy and astringent, while juice is their opposite: light, balanced, pleasant, strengthening, both food and medicine; their union displays divine power and mercy.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r1.anchor: فكلها باردة يابسة أرضية كثيفة قابضة عفصة قوية في هذه الصفات

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r2.claim: Since plant kinds are too numerous to describe, God names four of the noblest as a cue to the rest.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r2.anchor: أنواع النبات أكثر من أن تفي بشرحها مجلدات ،

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r3.claim: One explanation is that fruits may match in color and shape yet differ in taste, or differ in appearance yet share flavor and pleasure.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r3.anchor: قد تكون متشابهة في اللون والشكل ، مع أنها تكون مختلفة في الطعم واللذة

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r4.claim: Another explanation is that peel and seeds across many fruits resemble one another in taste and properties, while their flesh and moisture differ in taste.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r4.anchor: أن أكثر الفواكه يكون ما فيها من القشر والعجم متشابها في الطعم والخاصية

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r5.speaker: قتادة
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r5.claim: Qatada says tree leaves are similar to one another, whereas their fruits differ.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r5.anchor: قال قتادة : أوراق الأشجار تكون قريبة من التشابه

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r6.speaker: بعضهم
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r6.claim: An additional explanation says the trees resemble one another while their fruits differ.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r6.anchor: ومنهم من يقول : الأشجار متشابهة والثمار مختلفة

RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r7.claim: Razi's example is one grape cluster: most berries are ripe, sweet and pleasant, while a few remain green, sour and astringent.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90/r7.anchor: تأخذ العنقود من العنب فترى جميع حباته مدركة نضيجة حلوة طيبة

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r1.claim: The verbs for being alike, اشتبه and تشابه, can mean the same as استوى and تساوى; the two verb patterns often overlap.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r1.anchor: يقال : اشتبه الشيآن وتشابها كقولك استويا وتساويا ، والافتعال والتفاعل يشتركان كثيرا

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r2.claim: An unnamed reading has متشابها وغير متشابه in place of the verse's wording.

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r3.claim: The singular مشتبها instead of a dual can either describe only one of the paired items or elide a repeated description, applying similarity and difference to both olive and pomegranate; a poetic line illustrates the construction.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r3.anchor: إنما قال مشتبها ولم يقل مشتبهين إما اكتفاء بوصف أحدهما

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r4.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r4.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ثمره with both ث and م vocalized u; it can be the plural of ثمرة, as خشبة becomes خشب, supported by Quran 63:4 and a line about hills.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r4.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي { ثمره } بضم الثاء والميم ،

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r5.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r5.claim: A second analysis of their reading makes ثمر a collective plural formed by first pluralizing ثمرة as ثمار and then pluralizing that collective.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r5.anchor: أن يكون جمع ثمرة على ثمار . ثم جمع ثمارا على ثمر فيكون ثمر جمع الجمع

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r6.speaker: أبو عمرو
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r6.claim: Abu Amr reads ثمره with ث vocalized u and م unvocalized, explained as a lightened form, like the differing vocalization of رسل.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r6.anchor: وأما قراءة أبي عمرو فوجهها أن تخفيف ثمر ثمر كقولهم : رسل ورسل

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r7.speaker: الباقون
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r7.claim: The remaining readers open both consonants; ثمر is then the collective plural of ثمرة, like بقرة/بقر, شجرة/شجر and خرزة/خرز.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r7.anchor: وأما قراءة الباقين فوجهها : أن الثمر جمع ثمرة

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r8.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r8.anchor: والبحث الثاني : قال الواحدي : الينع النضج

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة والليث
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda gives yaneʿ/yīneʿ with fatḥa in the past and kasra in the present; al-Layth lists yanat, ayneʿat and forms with both ya vowels, plus participles yāniʿ and mūniʿ.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r9.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : يقال ينع يينع ، بالفتح في الماضي والكسر في المستقبل . وقال الليث :

RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r10.speaker: صاحب الكشاف وابن محيصن
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r10.claim: Al-Zamakhshari notes a reading with yaḍamma in وينعه; Ibn Muhaysin reads ويانعه.
RAZI-FULL:v13p90#2/r10.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : وقرىء { وينعه } بضم الياء ، وقرأ ابن محيصن { * ويانعه }

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r1.claim: Looking at the fruit when it first appears examines its beginning; looking at ripeness examines its completion, which is the main proof intended by the verse.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r1.anchor: أمر بالنظر في حال الثمر في أول حدوثها . وقوله : { وينعه } أمر بالنظر

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r2.claim: Fruits and blossoms change from their initial qualities to opposites as they mature: green turns dark or red, sour turns sweet, and sometimes cold becomes hot.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r2.anchor: لا تبقى على حالاتها الأولى ، بل تنتقل إلى أحوال مضادة للأحوال السابقة ، مثل أنها كانت

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r3.claim: These diverse changes need a cause; because nature, seasons, stars and spheres relate similarly to unlike bodies, they cannot explain different outcomes, which must be attributed to a choosing, wise and merciful governor.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r3.anchor: النسب المتشابهة لا يمكن أن تكون أسبابا لحدوث الحوادث المختلفة

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r4.speaker: القاضي
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r4.claim: Al-Qadi says the signs address those seeking faith in God, since the evidence is available to believer and unbeliever alike.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r4.anchor: قال القاضي : المراد لمن يطلب الإيمان بالله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r5.claim: Another possibility is that believers alone are named because they benefit from the sign, as with the description of guidance for the mindful in 2:2.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r5.anchor: وجه تخصيص المؤمنين بالذكر أنهم الذين انتفعوا به دون غيرهم

RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r6.claim: Razi says the sign proves a capable, choosing God clearly, yet benefits only those for whom God decrees faith; those decreed to unbelief gain nothing from it.
RAZI-FULL:v13p91/r6.anchor: قوة الدليل لا تفيد ولا تنفع إلا إذا قدر الله للعبد حصول الإيمان

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r1.claim: Rain from heaven is a sign of Divine Power and Benevolence that revives the earth.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r1.anchor: God’s sending down water from the sky is repeatedly mentioned as a sign of Divine Power and Benevolence through which He revives the earth

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r2.claim: Rain also supplies human beings with drink.

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r3.claim: Water can purify people and remove Satan’s defilement.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r3.anchor: gives them a means to “purify” themselves and remove the defilement of Satan

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r4.claim: The Quran often describes water as the means by which diverse crops and fruits emerge from the earth.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r4.anchor: specifically cited as the means by which diverse crops and fruits come forth from the earth

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r5.claim: The verse shifts from third-person reference to God sending rain to first-person plural speech about bringing forth plants.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r5.anchor: The verse begins with a reference to God in the third person

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r6.claim: The distant third person evokes God’s Transcendence, while the intimate first person evokes His Immanence in every detail of earthly life.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r6.anchor: evokes God’s Transcendence relative to the earthly realm and His Immanence in all of its minute workings

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r7.claim: The variety of fruit produced by the same water invites wonder.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r7.anchor: wonder that such diverse fruits and produce come forth after being watered with the same water

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r8.claim: The verse evokes God’s power to produce multiplicity from singularity, as He creates many human beings from one soul.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r8.anchor: ability to bring forth diversity and multiplicity from singularity, as when He creates the multiplicity of human beings from a single soul

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r9.claim: Other verses cite grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates as abundant provision, sometimes in the heavenly Garden.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r9.anchor: are also found in other verses as examples of God’s bountiful provision in the world and, in some cases, in the heavenly Garden

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r10.claim: Earthly fruits and the fruits of Paradise are symbolically analogous or comparable.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r10.anchor: the fruits of the earth and of Paradise are symbolically analogous or comparable

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r11.claim: Low-hanging date clusters suggest bounty and ease because heavy, ripe fruit is readily accessible.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r11.anchor: Clusters of dates hanging low suggests both bounty and ease, as the fruit hangs low when it is heavy and ripe

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r12.claim: Plants can resemble one another even when their produce differs greatly.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r12.anchor: the resemblance certain plants have to one another, even when their produce is very different

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r13.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r13.claim: The resemblance and difference of produce evoke the interwoven oneness and multiplicity of creation.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r13.anchor: the interwoven nature of oneness and multiplicity in creation

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r14.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r14.claim: The signs in creation point to God’s Oneness, Power, and Wisdom.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r14.anchor: signs of God’s Oneness, Power, and Wisdom

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r15.claim: Those who believe are implicitly linked with those who know in verse 97 and understand in verse 98.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r15.anchor: phrase implicitly linked to a people who know in v. 97 and a people who understand in v. 98

STUDYQURAN:6:99/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r16.claim: Believers alone benefit from these signs by recognizing proofs of Divine Power and Oneness; disbelievers cannot grasp them.
STUDYQURAN:6:99/r16.anchor: those who believe are the real beneficiaries of these signs, for they alone are able to see in these signs the proofs of Divine Power and Oneness

TAB-FULL:v9p444/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r1.claim: The one who sends down water and produces provision is God, whose worship is due exclusively and without any partner.
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r1.anchor: والله الذي له العبادة خالصة لا شركة فيه لشيء سواه، هو الإله

TAB-FULL:v9p444/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r2.claim: Rain produces nourishment for livestock, birds, wild animals, and people: the food on which they feed and grow.
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r2.anchor: من غذاء الأنعام والبهائم والطير والوحش، وأرزاق بني آدم وأقواتهم ما يتغذون به ويأكلونه

TAB-FULL:v9p444/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r3.claim: “The vegetation of every thing” means what grows by the water, develops on it, and is sustained by it.
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r3.anchor: فأخرجنا به ما ينبت به كل شيء وينمو عليه ويصلح

TAB-FULL:v9p444/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r4.claim: It is also possible to take “every thing” as all kinds of plants, though al-Ṭabarī says the preceding interpretation is correct.
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r4.anchor: ولو قيل معناه: فأخرجنا به نبات جميع أنواع النبات، فيكون كل شيء هو أصناف النبات، كان مذهبا

TAB-FULL:v9p444/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r5.claim: The passage describes God's abundant provision through rain and plants, establishing His exclusive claim to worship.
TAB-FULL:v9p444/r5.anchor: هو الإله {الذي أنزل من السماء ماء فأخرجنا به نبات كل شيء}

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r1.claim: Qinwān are date clusters from the palm's spathe, hanging nearby and low.

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r2.claim: Qinwān is raised as the subject of the clause; it is the plural of qinw, just as ṣinw yields ṣinwān, and denotes a date cluster.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r2.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {من طلعها قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] قال: «عذوق متهدلة»

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r3.claim: The singular has the forms qinw and qanā; the dual and plural include qinwān, while the small plural is aqnāʾ.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r3.anchor: لها ذنب كالقنو قد مذلت به … وأسحم للتخطار بعد التشذر

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r4.claim: Qinwān and qiniyān distinguish regional usage: the first is Hijazi and Qaysi, while Tamīm uses qiniyān; Imruʾ al-Qays's verse attests qinwān.

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r5.claim: An unattributed poem uses qinw in its simile for a tail.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r5.anchor: لها ذنب كالقنو قد مذلت به … وأسحم للتخطار بعد التشذر

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the low-hanging clusters are on short palms, nearly touching the ground.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r6.anchor: عن ابن عباس: {قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] : " يعني بالقنوان الدانية: قصار النخل لاصقة عذوقها بالأرض "

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r7.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r7.claim: Qatāda explains the phrase as hanging clusters.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r7.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {من طلعها قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] قال: «عذوق متهدلة»

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r8.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r8.claim: Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib glosses dāniya as near.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r8.anchor: عن البراء، في قوله: {قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] قال: «قريبة»

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r9.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes the palms' clusters as drooping from the spathe.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r9.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قوله: {ومن النخل من طلعها قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] قال: «الدانية لتهدل العذوق من الطلع»

TAB-FULL:v9p446/r10.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r10.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r10.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the palms are short and close to the earth, and calls their spathe qinwān.
TAB-FULL:v9p446/r10.anchor: سمعت الضحاك، يقول في قوله: {ومن النخل من طلعها قنوان دانية} [الأنعام: 99] : يعني: " النخل القصار الملتزقة بالأرض، والقنوان: طلعه "

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r1.claim: The phrase describes grape gardens or vineyards.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r1.anchor: وجنات من أعناب والزيتون والرمان مشتبها وغير متشابه

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r2.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports the general reciters' accusative reading of jannāt, with the feminine plural ending in kasra despite its accusative case.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r2.anchor: والقراءة التي لا أستجيز أن يقرأ ذلك إلا بها النصب {وجنات من أعناب} [الأنعام: 99]

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r3.speaker: الأعمش
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r3.claim: Al-Aʿmash, on the authority of Ḥamza, is reported to read jannāt in the nominative, coordinating its case with qinwān despite their different kinds.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r3.anchor: عن الكسائي، قال: أخبرنا حمزة، عن الأعمش، أنه قرأ: (وجنات من أعناب) بالرفع فرفع (جنات) على إتباعها (القنوان) في الإعراب

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r4.claim: A cited line coordinates “a spear” with “a sword” in the same case as an analogy for alternate coordination.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r4.anchor: ورأيت زوجك في الوغى … متقلدا سيفا ورمحا

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r5.claim: Al-Ṭabarī permits only the accusative reading, citing the reciters' consensus and judging the nominative distant from the correct sense.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r5.anchor: والقراءة التي لا أستجيز أن يقرأ ذلك إلا بها النصب {وجنات من أعناب} [الأنعام: 99]

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r6.claim: Olives and pomegranates are coordinated with the gardens in meaning: God also produced olive and pomegranate trees and their fruit.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r6.anchor: عطف بالزيتون على (الجنات) بمعنى: وأخرجنا الزيتون والرمان مشتبها وغير متشابه

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r7.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r7.claim: Qatāda explains the plants as similar in foliage but different in fruit.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r7.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وجنات من أعناب والزيتون والرمان مشتبها وغير متشابه} [الأنعام: 99] قال: «مشتبها ورقه، مختلفا ثمره»

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r8.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r8.claim: The phrase can mean that the trees resemble one another in form but differ in taste; “olive and pomegranate” names their fruits while omitting “trees.”
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r8.anchor: وشجر الزيتون والرمان، فاكتفى من ذكر الشجر بذكر ثمره

TAB-FULL:v9p448/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r9.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r9.claim: Omitting the people when saying “ask the town” in 12:82 is a parallel ellipsis, with the intended referent understood from context.
TAB-FULL:v9p448/r9.anchor: كما قيل: {واسأل القرية} [يوسف: 82] ، فاكتفى بذكر القرية من ذكر أهلها

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r1.speaker: قراء المدينة وبعض البصرة
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r1.claim: Medinan reciters and some Basrans read thamar with fatḥa on both consonants.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r1.anchor: قرأته عامة قراء أهل المدينة وبعض أهل البصرة: {انظروا إلى ثمره} [الأنعام: 99] بفتح الثاء والميم

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r2.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفيون
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r2.claim: Some Meccan and most Kufan reciters read thumuruhu with ḍamma on both consonants.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r2.anchor: وقرأه بعض قراء أهل مكة وعامة قراء الكوفيين: (إلى ثمره) بضم الثاء والميم

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r3.claim: With fatḥa, thamar is the plural of thamara, like qaṣab from qaṣaba and khashab from khashaba, referring to the fruits of the named trees.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r3.anchor: وأن الثمر جمع ثمرة، كما القصب جمع قصبة، والخشب جمع خشبة

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r4.claim: With ḍamma, thumur is a plural of thimār, analogous to ḥumur from ḥimār and jirab from jirāb.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r4.anchor: وجه ذلك إلى أنه جمع ثمار، كما الحمر جمع حمار، والجرب جمع جراب

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r5.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r5.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read thumuruhu and glossed it as kinds of wealth.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r5.anchor: عن يحيى بن وثاب، أنه كان يقرأ: (إلى ثمره) يقول: «هو أصناف المال»

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r6.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r6.claim: Mujāhid distinguishes thamar as wealth from thamar as the fruit of date palms.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r6.anchor: عن مجاهد، قال: " الثمر: هو المال، والثمر: ثمر النخل "

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r7.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r7.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the ḍamma reading because the verse gathers many kinds of produce and wealth—grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r7.anchor: وأولى القراءتين في ذلك عندي بالصواب، قراءة من قرأ: {انظروا إلى ثمره} [الأنعام: 99] بضم الثاء والميم

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r8.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r8.claim: Produce is aggregated through the forms thamara, thamar, and thimār; ithmār means setting fruit.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r8.anchor: فجمعت الثمرة ثمرا، ثم جمع الثمر ثمارا، ثم جمع ذلك فقيل: (انظروا إلى ثمره)

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r9.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r9.claim: Yanʿ means the fruit's ripening and reaching maturity.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r9.anchor: وأما قوله: {وينعه} [الأنعام: 99] فإنه: نضجه وبلوغه حين يبلغ

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r10.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r10.speaker: أهل البصرة
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r10.claim: Some Basran Arabists take the fatḥa pronunciation of yanʿ as a plural of yāniʿ, like tajr for tājir and ṣaḥb for ṣāḥib.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r10.anchor: كان بعض أهل العلم بكلام العرب من أهل البصرة يقول في ينعه: إذا فتحت ياؤه: هو جمع يانع

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r11.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r11.speaker: أهل الكوفة
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r11.claim: Some Kufan Arabists instead analyze yanʿ as a verbal noun of “the fruit ripened,” with three reported vowel patterns; they also give variants for the noun “ripeness.”
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r11.anchor: وكان بعض أهل الكوفة ينكر ذلك ويرى أنه مصدر من قولهم: ينع الثمر فهو يينع ينعا

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r12.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r12.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r12.claim: A reading with yāniʿihi means “its ripe, mature fruit.”
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r12.anchor: وأما في قراءة من قرأ ذلك: (ويانعه) ، فإنه يعني به: وناضجه وبالغه

TAB-FULL:v9p450/r13.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r13.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r13.claim: The verbal noun can also be yānūʿ; Arabs say the fruit has ripened, and a cited poem uses yanʿ.
TAB-FULL:v9p450/r13.anchor: ومسموع عند العرب: أينعت الثمرة تونع إيناعا

TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r1.claim: The poem's “olive has ripened” attests the Arabic verbal form yanʿ.

TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains yanʿ as ripening.

TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r3.anchor: عن قتادة: {انظروا إلى ثمره إذا أثمر وينعه} [الأنعام: 99] : «أي نضجه»

TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r4.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r4.claim: Al-Suddī explains the word as ripeness.

TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r5.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also glosses yanʿ as ripeness.
TAB-FULL:v9p450#2/r5.anchor: سمعت الضحاك، يقول في قوله: {وينعه} [الأنعام: 99] قال: يعني: «نضجه»

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r5.claim: Al-samāʾ means the upper direction: anything above and shading a person counts as sky.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r5.anchor: السماء هي جهة العلو فكلما علاك وأظلك فهو سماء

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r6.claim: On the cited explanation, water brings forth plant growth in everything capable of growth, unfolding from latency to manifestation; this includes plants, trees, humans, and other animals.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r6.anchor: فأخرجنا بالماء الذي أنزلناه من السماء النبات والنمو الذي في كل شيء نام له قوة النبات من الكمون إلى البروز

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r7.claim: Khidr means green and may be a shortened form of khāḍir.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r7.anchor: والخضر هو الأخضر وكأنه مخفف الخاضر

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r8.claim: The grains are described as stacked one above another, as in an ear of grain.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r8.anchor: وتراكب الحب انعقاد بعضه فوق بعض كما في السنبلة

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r9.claim: Ṭalʿ is the first fruit appearing on a date palm; qinwān is the plural of qinw, a date cluster like a grape cluster, and dāniya means near.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r9.anchor: والطلع أول ما يبدو من ثمر النخل والقنوان جمع قنو وهو العذق بالكسر

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r10.claim: The fruits are similar or dissimilar in kind, shape, and other respects; yanuʿ means the fruit’s ripening.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r10.anchor: والمشتبه وغير المتشابه المشاكل وغير المشاكل في النوع والشكل وغيرهما

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r11.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r11.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r11.claim: The examples are signs for people with insight to infer God’s oneness: earthly growth, celestial bodies, humanity’s origin, and the combined system of rain, food, and growing life.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r11.anchor: وقد ذكر الله سبحانه أمورا مما خلقه لينظر فيها من له نظر وبصيرة فيهتدي بالنظر فيها إلى توحيده

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r12.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r12.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r12.claim: The verse pairs each kind of sign with a capacity: stars address people who know, human creation those who understand deeply, and the growing system those who believe.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r12.anchor: وقد عد النجوم آية خاصة بقوم يعلمون، وإنشاء النفوس الإنسانية آية خاصة بقوم يفقهون، وتدبير نظام الإنبات آية لقوم يؤمنون

TABATABAI:6:99-100/r13.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r13.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r13.claim: The order of growth is readily grasped by ordinary understanding when free from stubbornness; celestial arrangements require specialist knowledge, while human creation calls for theoretical inquiry and deep inward scrutiny.
TABATABAI:6:99-100/r13.anchor: فإن النظر في أمر النظام أمر بسيط لا يفتقر إلى مؤونة زائدة بل يناله الفهم العادي

AKHFASH:v1p307/r5.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p307/r5.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p307/r5.claim: خضرا means the green growth, al-akhdar, supported by the Arab expression أَرِنيها نَمرة أَرَكها مَطرة.
AKHFASH:v1p307/r5.anchor: يريد "الأخضر" كقول العرب: "أرنيها نمرة أركها مطرة"

AKHFASH:v1p307/r6.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p307/r6.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p307/r6.claim: وجنات من أعناب continues the implied verb: We brought forth gardens of grapes by the water as well.
AKHFASH:v1p307/r6.anchor: ثم قال {وجنات من أعناب} أي: "وأخرجنا به جنات من أعناب"

AKHFASH:v1p307/r7.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p307/r7.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p307/r7.claim: The singular of قنوان is قنو, and the singular of الصنوان is صنو.

TABRISI:6:99/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r1.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم برواية أبي يوسف الأعشى والبرجمي وعلي بن أبي طالب وعبد الله بن مسعود والأعمش ويحيى بن يعمر
TABRISI:6:99/r1.claim: These readers use the nominative jannāt, coordinating it grammatically with qinwān by form even though the items differ in kind.
TABRISI:6:99/r1.anchor: قرأ أبو بكر عن عاصم برواية أبي يوسف الأعشى والبرجمي وجنات بالرفع وهو قراءة أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب

TABRISI:6:99/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r2.speaker: الباقون
TABRISI:6:99/r2.claim: The remaining readers use the accusative jannāt, coordinating it with khidran.

TABRISI:6:99/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r3.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف
TABRISI:6:99/r3.claim: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read thumuri with two ḍammas, including the occurrences in the commands to eat and in Yā Sīn.
TABRISI:6:99/r3.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف ثمره بضمتين وكذلك كلوا من ثمره وفي سورة ياسين ليأكلوا من ثمره

TABRISI:6:99/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r4.speaker: الباقون
TABRISI:6:99/r4.claim: The remaining readers pronounce thamar with two fatḥas in all the cited occurrences.
TABRISI:6:99/r4.anchor: وقرأ الباقون ثمره بفتحتين في الجميع

TABRISI:6:99/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r5.claim: With accusative jannāt, the word coordinates with khidran: God brings forth green growth and grape gardens from the water.
TABRISI:6:99/r5.anchor: من قرأ وجنات فإنه عطفها على قوله خضرا

TABRISI:6:99/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r6.claim: The nominative jannāt coordinates with qinwān by grammatical form despite their different categories, as in the poet's pairing of a sword and spear.
TABRISI:6:99/r6.anchor: فإنه عطفها على قنوان لفظا وإن لم يكن من جنسها

TABRISI:6:99/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r7.claim: Thamar can be the singular collective, just as baqara/bāqir and shajara/shajar pair singular and collective forms.
TABRISI:6:99/r7.anchor: فالثمر جمع ثمرة مثل بقرة وبقر وشجرة وشجر

TABRISI:6:99/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r8.claim: The two-ḍamma reading can derive thumur from singular thamara like khashaba/khashab and akama/akam, as the poet's line illustrates.

TABRISI:6:99/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r9.claim: Alternatively, thumur is a collective plural of thimār, a plural of thamarah; qāra/qūr and nāqah/sāḥah/sūḥ offer analogous patterns.
TABRISI:6:99/r9.anchor: والآخر أن يكون جمع ثمار على ثمر فيكون ثمر جمع الجمع

TABRISI:6:99/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r10.claim: Khiḍr means green or fresh; Arabs also use akhḍar for black, call Iraq's lush land Sawād, and describe fertile, spacious people or places as green. A cited poem calls the poet green-skinned and a notable Arab.
TABRISI:6:99/r10.anchor: وقال الفضل بن عباس بن عتبة بن أبي لهب

TABRISI:6:99/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r11.claim: The hadith calls worldly life sweet and green, meaning tender and flourishing; the expressions 'his blood went green' and 'took it green' mean vainly and for free.
TABRISI:6:99/r11.anchor: أي غضة ناعمة وذهب دمه خضرا أي باطلا

TABRISI:6:99/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r12.claim: Mutarākib means piled or layered, from the form of rukūb.

TABRISI:6:99/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r13.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r13.claim: Ṭalʿ is the first emergence of the palm's fruit; qinwān is plural of qinw, a bunch or cluster, and dāniya means close at hand.
TABRISI:6:99/r13.anchor: والقنوان جمع قنو وهو العذق بكسر العين أي الكباسة

TABRISI:6:99/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99/r14.claim: Yanaʿ and yanʿ mean ripening; the poet's olives have ripened. Yanʿ may also be a plural like ṣāḥib/ṣaḥb and tājir/tajar.
TABRISI:6:99/r14.anchor: والينع والنضج يقال ينع الثمر ينعا وينعا وأينع إذا أدرك

TABRISI:6:99#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r1.claim: Here sky means cloud; in Arabic anything above that casts shade can be called samāʾ.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r1.anchor: يريد من السحاب والعرب تقول كل ما علاك فأطلك فهو سماء

TABRISI:6:99#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r2.claim: The water grows the food of livestock, birds, wild animals, and humans, sustaining their nourishment and growth; this is preferable to taking the phrase as all botanical kinds.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r2.anchor: والأول أحسن وإنما قال به لأنه سبحانه جعله سببا مؤديا إلى النبات لا مولدا له

TABRISI:6:99#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r3.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:6:99#2/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows that the phrase means all varieties of plants, taking kull shayʾ as botanical species, as in the cited verse.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r3.anchor: المراد أخرجنا به من جميع أنواع النبات

TABRISI:6:99#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r4.claim: Water is a means leading to growth, not an independently generative cause: God could have brought forth plants without it.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r4.anchor: جعله سببا مؤديا إلى النبات لا مولدا له وقد كان يمكنه الإنبات بغيره

TABRISI:6:99#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r5.claim: The green growth is a fresh green crop, the stalk of the grain ear; 'from it' is understood as from the water.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r5.anchor: فأخرجنا منه } أي من الماء. وقيل: من النبات

TABRISI:6:99#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r6.claim: The grain comes from the green crop, with its kernels layered one over another, as in wheat and sesame ears.

TABRISI:6:99#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r7.claim: God also brings forth bunches of ripe dates from the palms' flower clusters; the bunches are within reach.

TABRISI:6:99#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r8.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:6:99#2/r8.claim: The verse mentions nearby bunches and leaves distant ones implicit: as garments shielding from heat also shield from cold, the context supplies what is omitted.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r8.anchor: ولم يقل ومنها قنوان بعيدة لأن في الكلام دليلا على البعيدة السحيقة

TABRISI:6:99#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r9.speaker: غير مسمى
TABRISI:6:99#2/r9.claim: Another explanation is that abundant, heavy fruit pulls the bunches close to the ground.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r9.anchor: دانية دنت من الأرض لكثرة ثمرها وثقل حملها

TABRISI:6:99#2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r10.claim: The flower cluster is singled out because it bears fine, nourishing food unavailable in the fruit's outer casings.
TABRISI:6:99#2/r10.anchor: وإنما خص الطلع بالذكر لما فيه من المنافع والأغذية الشريفة التي ليست في أكمام الثمار

TABRISI:6:99#2/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#2/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#2/r11.claim: The water also brings forth grape orchards; in the nominative reading, the implied verb is 'We bring forth.'
TABRISI:6:99#2/r11.anchor: يعني وأخرجنا به أيضا جنات من أعناب أي بساتين

TABRISI:6:99#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#3/r1.claim: Olive and pomegranate refer to their trees; their leaves cover the branch from one end to the other, as the poet's ripened pomegranate and olives illustrate.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r1.anchor: ومعناه أن ورقهما يشتمل على العود كله

TABRISI:6:99#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#3/r2.claim: The trees resemble one another while differing in taste.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r2.anchor: أي مشتبها شجره يشبه بعضه بعضا وغير متشابه في الطعم

TABRISI:6:99#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r3.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:6:99#3/r3.claim: Qatāda says the leaves resemble one another while the fruits differ.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r3.anchor: مشتبها ورقه مختلفا ثمره عن قتادة

TABRISI:6:99#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r4.speaker: قول غير مسمى
TABRISI:6:99#3/r4.claim: Another reported view says the plants resemble one another in form but differ in taste.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r4.anchor: وقيل: مشتبها في الخلق مختلفا في الطعم

TABRISI:6:99#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r5.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:6:99#3/r5.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says things of one kind resemble one another, while things of different kinds do not.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r5.anchor: مشتبها ما كان من جنس واحد وغير متشابه إذا اختلف جنسه عن الجبائي

TABRISI:6:99#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#3/r6.claim: The best reading includes all the reported likenesses and differences: fruits resemble in some respects and differ in others.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r6.anchor: والأولى أن يقال أن جميع ذلك مشتبه من وجوه مختلف من وجوه فيدخل فيه جميع ما تقدم

TABRISI:6:99#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#3/r7.claim: Observe fruit from its first appearance to ripeness and how taste, color, smell, and size change; this reveals a maker who governs it.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r7.anchor: من ابتداء خروجه إذا أثمر إلى انتهائه إذا أينع وأدرك كيف تنتقل عليه الأحوال في الطعم واللون والرائحة

TABRISI:6:99#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:6:99#3/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:6:99#3/r8.claim: The well-formed crops and diverse fruits point to a creator who knowingly distinguished them before bringing them into being and governs their growth; believers benefit by drawing this inference.
TABRISI:6:99#3/r8.anchor: لدلالات على أن لها خالقا قصد إلى التمييز بينها قبل خلقها على علم بها

FARRA:v1p346/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r4.claim: نبات كل شيء means the provision each thing grows: plants suitable to nourish it; al-Farrāʾ calls this the proper interpretation.
FARRA:v1p346/r4.anchor: يقول: رزق كل شيء، يريد ما ينبت ويصلح غذاء لكل شيء.

FARRA:v1p346/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r5.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r5.claim: Arabic also permits construing نبات as annexed to كل شيء while intending vegetation belonging to all things, like حق اليقين where the two terms refer to one thing.
FARRA:v1p346/r5.anchor: وقد يجوز في العربية أن تضيف النبات إلى كل شيء وأنت تريد بكل شيء النبات أيضا،

FARRA:v1p346/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r6.claim: قنوان is properly nominative because the sense is “from the palms, their clusters are near.”
FARRA:v1p346/r6.anchor: وقوله: من النخل من طلعها قنوان دانية الوجه الرفع في القنوان

FARRA:v1p346/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r7.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r7.claim: An accusative construction is possible in speech but not read because of the written text.
FARRA:v1p346/r7.anchor: ولو نصب: وأخرج من النخل من طلعها قنوانا دانية لجاز في الكلام، ولا يقرأ

FARRA:v1p346/r8.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r8.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r8.claim: وجنات من أعناب is accusative; the sound feminine plural takes a genitive-looking kasra in the accusative, though raising it to coordinate with قنوان is also correct.
FARRA:v1p346/r8.anchor: وقوله: وجنات من أعناب نصب، إلا أن جمع المؤنث بالتاء يخفض

FARRA:v1p346/r9.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r9.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r9.claim: Raising the gardens to coordinate with قنوان is also correct.
FARRA:v1p346/r9.anchor: ولو رفعت الجنات تتبع القنوان كان صوابا.

FARRA:v1p346/r12.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r12.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r12.claim: Olive and pomegranate mean their trees here, just as “ask the town” means ask its inhabitants.
FARRA:v1p346/r12.anchor: وقوله: والزيتون والرمان يريد شجرة الزيتون وشجر الرمان،

FARRA:v1p346/r13.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r13.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r13.claim: The instruction is to inspect the fruit when it first forms and then watch its ripening.
FARRA:v1p346/r13.anchor: انظروا إلى ثمره إذا أثمر يقول: انظروا إليه أول ما يعقد

FARRA:v1p346/r14.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p346/r14.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p346/r14.claim: The word is read وينعه or يانعه: وينعه means its ripeness, while يانعه means ripe and fully grown.
FARRA:v1p346/r14.anchor: فأما قوله: وينعه فمثل نضجه، ويانعه مثل ناضجه وبالغه.

THALABI:v4p174/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p174/r1.speaker: أهل الكوفة
THALABI:v4p174/r1.claim: The Kufans read thamar with ḍamma on thāʾ and mīm, as a plural of thimār.
THALABI:v4p174/r1.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة: بضم الثاء والميم على جمع الثمار.

THALABI:v4p174/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p174/r2.speaker: الباقون
THALABI:v4p174/r2.claim: The other readers read it with fatḥa on both letters, as the plural of thamara, a single fruit.
THALABI:v4p174/r2.anchor: وقرأ الباقون بفتحهما على جمع الثمرة مثل بعر ووبر إذا أثمر

THALABI:v4p174/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p174/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p174/r3.claim: Yanʿ means the fruit’s ripening and maturity.

THALABI:v4p174/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p174/r4.speaker: أبو رجاء ومحمد بن السميقع
THALABI:v4p174/r4.claim: Abu Raja and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read yāniʿihi with an alif as a noun.
THALABI:v4p174/r4.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء ومحمد بن السميقع: ويانعه بالألف على الإسم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the water is rain, and every drop descends with an angel accompanying it.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: المطر الذي ينزل، ليس من نقطة إلا ومعها ملك)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r2.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r2.claim: Al-Farra's primary reading is that God brings forth the sustenance of every kind, meaning plants suitable as food for each kind.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r2.anchor: ذكر الفراء فيه قولين: (أحدهما يقول: رزق كل شيء، يريد: ما ينبت مما يصلح غذاء لكل شيء، قال: وكذا جاء التفسير

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r3.claim: Al-Farra also allows the Arabic construction to attach nabāt to kull shayʾ while intending every thing to mean plant, comparing 56:95.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r4.claim: Abu Ishaq says khaḍir has the same sense as akhḍar, as ʿawar corresponds to aʿwar.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r4.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (معنى خضر كمعنى أخضر، يقال: اخضر فهو أخضر وخضر، مثل اعور فهو أعور وعور)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r5.speaker: الليث وابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p316/r5.claim: Al-Layth says Qur'anic khaḍir means crops; Ibn Abbas lists wheat, sult, barley, corn, and rice as fresh green growth from such grains.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r1.claim: From the green growth God brings forth grains, stacked one upon another within a single ear.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r1.anchor: يعني: من الخضر، نخرج {حبا متراكبا} بعضه على بعض في سنبلة واحدة

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r2.claim: Abu Ubayda explains the palm's ṭalʿ as its early spathe before it splits to show the iġrīḍ; iġrīḍ is also called ṭalʿ, the first visible part of the cluster.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r2.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: (أطلعت النخلة إذا أخرجت طلعها، وطلعها كفراها

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r3.speaker: أبو زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r3.claim: Abu Zayd distinguishes the verb forms for a palm putting out ṭalʿ and ṭalʿ emerging.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r3.anchor: قال أبو زيد: (أطلع النخل الطلع إطلاعا، وطلع الطلع يطلع طلوعا)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r4.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj says qinwān is the plural of qinw, patterned on ṣinw and ṣinwān; its dual has a kasra on the nūn.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r4.anchor: قال الزجاج: (جمع قنو، مثل صنو وصنوان، وإذا ثنيت القنو قلت: قنوان، بكسر النون)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r5.claim: Abu Ubayda says the plural comes in a dual-like form, with the nūn inflection marking plurality, a pattern without another Arabic example.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r5.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: (ثم جاء جمعه على لفظ الاثنين مثل صنو وصنوان، والإعراب في النون للجمع، وليس لهما في كلام العرب نظير)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r6.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays's verse uses qinwān of date clusters, serving as poetic evidence for the word.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r6.anchor: قال امرؤ القيس (¬5): فأثت أعاليه وآدت أصوله ... ومال بقنوان من البسر أحمرا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r7.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r7.claim: Abu Ali says the kasra in qinwān is introduced by plural formation, not retained from qinw; he compares hījān and ẓirāf.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r7.anchor: قال أبو علي: الكسرة التي في (قنوان) ليست التي كانت في قنو

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says the clusters hang from the palm's flower stalk and dāniya means close to the picker; he also reports short palms whose clusters touch the ground.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r9.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r9.claim: Abu Ishaq defines dāniya as easy to reach; mention of nearby clusters implies distant ones, just as garments protecting from heat also protect from cold.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p317/r9.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ({دانية} أي: قريبة المتناول، قال: ولم يقل: ومنها قنوان بعيدة

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r1.claim: The preferred reading puts jannāt in the accusative, coordinated with khaḍiran as the object of "We brought forth."
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r1.anchor: لأنها في موضع نصب نسقا على قوله (خضرا) أي: فأخرجنا خضرا {وجنات من أعناب}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r2.speaker: الأعشى عن أبي بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r2.claim: Al-Aʿsha transmits a reading from Abu Bakr with jannāt in the nominative.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r3.claim: Ibn al-Anbari offers two analyses of the nominative: an implied verb makes the gardens an object, or they coordinate with qinwān by proximity despite not growing from palm clusters.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r3.anchor: ابن الأنباري: (وله مذهبان أحدهما: أن يكون الجنات مفعولة في

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r4.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r4.claim: For the second analysis, he cites poetry coordinating eyes with eyebrows by proximity even though eyes are not plucked or shaped.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r4.anchor: والمذهب الآخر: رفع الجنات بالنسق على القنوان؛ تغليبا لمعنى الجوار، كما قال الشاعر: وزججن الحواجب والعيونا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r5.speaker: الفرزدق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r5.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line raises al-khamr as an object, supporting the construction with an implied verb.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r5.anchor: قال الفرزدق: غداة أحلت لابن أصرم طعنة ... حصين عبيطات السدائف والخمر

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r6.speaker: الشاعر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r6.claim: The poetic example illustrates coordination by proximity; eyes are not themselves plucked or shaped.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p320/r6.anchor: كما قال الشاعر: وزججن الحواجب والعيونا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r1.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r1.claim: Al-Farra takes olive and pomegranate to mean their trees, just as "ask the town" means ask its people.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r1.anchor: قال الفراء: (يريد: شجر الزيتون، وشجر الرمان، كما قال: {واسأل القرية}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r2.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل وأكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r2.claim: Qatada, Muqatil, and most commentators say the leaves resemble one another while the fruits differ.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r3.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj instead says the trees resemble one another but differ in taste.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r3.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (أي: شجره، يشبه بعضه بعضا {وغير متشابه} في الطعم)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r4.speaker: عبد العزيز بن يحيى
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r4.claim: Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya says the command to look means to examine as evidence and draw a lesson.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r4.anchor: قال عبد العزيز بن يحيى: (نظر الاستدلال والعبرة)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r5.speaker: أبو روق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r5.claim: Abu Rوق reads the command as an invitation to consider and take admonition.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r6.claim: Al-Farra says "when it bears fruit" means when fruit first forms.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r6.anchor: قال الفراء: (يقول: انظروا إليه أول ما يعقد)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r7.claim: Thamar is a collective plural of thamara, like baqara/baqr and shajara/shajar, and it also has broken plurals on the fiʿāl pattern.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r7.anchor: والثمر: جمع ثمرة مثل: بقرة وبقر وشجرة وشجر وجزرة وجزر، وقد كسروها على فعال

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r8.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r8.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read thumur with ḍamma on both consonants; the clearest analysis makes it a plural of thamara like khashaba/khashab and akama/ukum.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r8.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي (ثمره) بضم الثاء (¬1) والميم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r9.claim: A second possible analysis derives thumur by making thimar a plural of thamara and then forming a plural of that plural.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r9.anchor: والوجه الآخر: أن يكون جمع ثمرة على ثمار، ثم جمع ثمارا على ثمر، فيكون ثمر جمع الجمع

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r10.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses ukum for plural akama, illustrating the reading's plural pattern.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p322/r10.anchor: قال: ترى الأكم منه (¬4) سجدا للحوافر

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r1.claim: Yanʿ means ripeness; Abu Ubayda says yanaʿa has fatḥa in the past and kasra in the present, as shown by a poetic line.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r1.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: (يقال: ينع يينع بالفتح في الماضي والكسر في المستقبل)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r2.claim: He cites an anonymous line using the olive as having ripened, attesting yanʿ.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r3.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r3.claim: Al-Layth records alternate forms for fruit ripening, including yanʿa and aynʿat, their verbal nouns, and the participles yāniʿ and mūniʿ.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r3.anchor: وقال الليث: (ينعت الثمرة، بالكسر، وأينعت، فهي [تينع] (¬1) وتونع إيناعا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r4.claim: The signs are for those who believe that the one who brought forth the plants can revive and resurrect the dead.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r4.anchor: يريد: يصدقون أن الذي أخرج هذا النبات قادر على أن يحيى الموتى ويبعثهم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r5.claim: Abu Ishaq argues that God alone can move creation through these changing states, so the same God can resurrect people who denied resurrection.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v8p324/r5.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬4): (احتج الله عز وجل بتصريف ما خلق، ونقله من حال إلى حال

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r1.claim: Qinwān means palm clusters and is the plural of qinw; the plural keeps the pattern's nūn vowels, unlike the dual, as in ṣinw and ṣinwān.
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r1.anchor: (القنوان) عذوق النخل. واحدها قنو. جمع على لفظ تثنيته

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r2.claim: The fruit at the time it first appears is tender and unripe.
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r2.anchor: انظروا إلى ثمره إذا أثمر} وهو غض.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r3.claim: Yanʿ means the fruit's ripening and maturity; the verb can be yāniʿat or aynʿat, and the noun has several forms.
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p157#4/r3.anchor: وينعه} أي إدراكه ونضجه. يقال: ينعت الثمرة وأيعنت: إذا أدركت.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r1.claim: Rain from the sky brings forth every kind of plant.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r1.anchor: { وهو الذي أنزل من السماء ماء } يعني: المطر

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r2.claim: Green growth includes wheat, barley, corn, and other moist green growth from grain plants.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r2.anchor: { فأخرجنا } من ذلك النبات { خضرا } أخضر، كالقمح، والشعير، والذرة، وما كان رطبا أخضر مما ينبت من الحبوب

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r3.claim: The grain is layered one over another in a single ear.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r3.anchor: { نخرج منه } من الخضر { حبا متراكبا } بعضه على بعض في سنبلة واحدة

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r4.claim: The first emerging palm shoot bears hanging clusters; low palms have bunches near the ground and easy to pick.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r4.anchor: { ومن النخل من طلعها } أول ما يطلع منها { قنوان } يعني: العراجين التي قد تدلت من الطلع { دانية }

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r5.claim: The gardens include grapes, olive trees, and pomegranate trees, brought forth by water.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r5.anchor: { وجنات } أي: وأخرجنا بالماء جنات { من أعناب والزيتون } وشجر الزيتون { والرمان } وشجر الرمان

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r6.claim: The fruits resemble one another in color, specifically pomegranates, but differ in taste.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r6.anchor: { مشتبها } [في اللون: يعني: الرماني] { وغير متشابه } [في الطعم. أي: مختلفة في الطعم.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r7.speaker: قيل
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r7.claim: Another explanation is that the leaves resemble one another while the fruits differ.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r8.claim: Look for reflection and inference when fruit first forms and ripens.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r8.anchor: { انظروا إلى ثمره } نظر الاستدلال والعبرة أول ما يعقد { وينعه } نضجه

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r9.claim: These signs show believers that the One who brings forth plants can also bring the dead to life.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:6:99/r9.anchor: { إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يؤمنون } يصدقون أن الذي أخرج هذا النبات قادر على أن يحيي الموتى.

ELMALILI:6:98-99/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99/r3.claim: His rendering describes rain bringing out every kind of vegetation, then green growth and stacked grain, hanging date clusters, grape gardens, olives, and pomegranates; it invites observing fruit from first growth to ripeness.
ELMALILI:6:98-99/r3.anchor: semâdan bir su indirdi, derken onunla her şeyin nebatını çıkardık. Derken ondan bir yeşillik çıkardık, ondan birbiri üzerine binmiş dâneler çıkarıyoruz.

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r8.claim: God sends down water and brings forth the vegetation of every thing, activating growth and development in plants and in things nourished or transformed through plant life.
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r8.anchor: Habb ü nevâtın ve her türlü nebâtın ve insanlar ve hayvanlar gibi nebat ile tegaddî eden veya me‘âdin vesâire gibi nebâtâta gıda olarak onlara tehavvül ve temessül edecek olan her şeyin nebâtiyetini

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r9.claim: From the plant or thing God brings forth fresh green growth, from which stacked grains emerge.
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r9.anchor: ve binâen‘aleyh ondan, o nebattan veya o şeyden taze bir yeşillik, bir çim çıkardık.

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r10.claim: The close-packed grain ears resemble cavalry companies lined for battle, their spears extended against an attack from the air.
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r10.anchor: mızraklarını uzatmış süvari bölükleri gibi ne güzel müterâkibdirler

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r11.claim: Date palms produce nearby hanging clusters from their spathes; the verse also names grape gardens, olives, and pomegranates.
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r11.anchor: yani tomurcuğundan da {قِنْوَانٌۭ دَانِيَةٌۭ} yakınlara sarkmış salkımlar olur.

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r12.claim: The fruits' likeness and difference restate more plainly the rule of regularity and variation signaled earlier by settled and deposited states.
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r12.anchor: Bu müşabehet ve ‘adem-i müşabehet kaydı, yukarıda istikrar ve istîda‘ile ifade olunan

ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:6:98-99#3/r13.claim: Compare a fruit when it first appears, still unripe, with its maturity: their difference displays nurture and a clear course of development, signs for believers of God's existence, unity, power, and providential wisdom.
